title: PCA-based supervised identification of biological soil crusts in multispectral images
author: Fischer

steps.title: Load required R packages and define functions
steps.instruction: In R, load the gatepoints and jpeg packages, then create two functions: plot_jpeg for displaying image objects and plot_PCA for reallocating classification results to image coordinates (code provided in supplementary information).

steps.title: Import RGB and NIR images and record dimensions
steps.instruction: Read the calibrated RGB image (imageRGB.jpg) and the registered NIR image (imageNIR-reg.jpg) with readJPEG, assign them to imgRGB.stat and imgNIR.stat, and store their x‑y dimensions in variable res as the first two elements of dim(imgRGB.stat).

steps.title: Construct hypercube and reshape to 1‑D matrix
steps.instruction: Combine the three channels of the RGB image and the three channels of the NIR image into a 3‑D array named imgMult whose z‑dimension equals the sum of the channel counts of both images; then flatten imgMult to a 2‑D array imgMult.1d with rows equal to res[1]*res[2] and columns equal to (dim(imgRGB.stat)[3] + dim(imgNIR.stat)[3]).

substeps.instruction: imgMult <- array(c(imgRGB.stat[,,1:3], imgNIR.stat[,,1:3]), dim = c(res[1], res[2], (dim(imgRGB.stat)[3] + dim(imgNIR.stat)[3])))

steps.title: Perform principal component analysis
steps.instruction: Run PCA on imgMult.1d with scaling (scale. = TRUE) using prcomp, storing the result in img.PCA; for the example images the first two components explained 9615% of the total variance.

steps.title: Generate PC1‑PC2 density plot and data frame
steps.instruction: Create a data frame kk2 containing the scores of PC1 and PC2 from img.PCA, then produce a smoothScatter density plot of these two components.

steps.title: Select spectral features with freehand polygon and visualize
steps.instruction: Use the fhs function from gatepoints to outline polygons on the PC1‑PC2 scatter (kk2), setting names = FALSE and pch = NA_integer_; points inside polygons are marked TRUE, others FALSE. Close the selection with a right‑click, then display the binary classification with plot_PCA, which renders selected pixels in white and all others in black.

substeps.instruction: selectedPoints <- fhs(kk2, names = FALSE, pch = NA_integer_)

description: The multispectral approach in remote sensing typically includes the estimation of spectral indices. For biocrusts, the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI [1,2]) has been proposed; however, high NDVI values of wet biocrusts may be misinterpreted as vascular plant vegetation dynamics whereas dry biocrusts only gained negligible NDVI values [3]. To overcome this disadvantage, several more specific spectral indices have been proposed for biocrusts, like the crust index (CI, respectively [4]), the brightness index (BI [5]) or the biological soil crust index (BSCI [6]), where biocrusts are characterized by typical ranges of respective index values. All spectral indices well reflect crust activity or biomass but are not specific enough to differentiate between different crust types, like lichen, cyanobacterial, algal or moss biocrusts. Rodriguez-Caballero et al. [7] propose support vector machines (SVM) for supervised classification of biocrusts from hyperspectral remote sensing data. However, a common problem with linear spectral mixture analysis (SMA) remains when the number of spectral endmembers is greater than the number actually required to unmix an individual pixel in the scene [3]. Non-spectral unsupervised principal component analysis (PCA) classification of biocrusts has indicated that the development of the microbial community was affected at multiple scales, including biocrust successional stage, seasonal effect and the micro-geomorphology [8]. High-resolution VIS-NIR spectroscopy was employed to study the influence of wetting on cyanolichen-dominated biocrusts in a non-imaging approach [7]. There was no attempt so far in the literature to use multispectral PCA classification of biocrusts in high-resolution images. The method proposed refers to Rodarmel and Shan [9] who suggested principal component analysis for preprocessing of hyperspectral images.
